Consider the strange gift of starlight. The photons striking your retina tonight may have left their home stars decades—or millennia—before you were born. When you look up at the night sky, you're not seeing the universe as it is. You're reading old mail, envelopes postmarked centuries ago by objects that may no longer exist at all.

But this is true of everything, not just stars. All vision is time travel. The friend sitting across from you exists, for your purposes, slightly in your past: light takes a few nanoseconds to cross the table, and your brain needs far longer than that to assemble those signals into a face. We never experience "now" directly. We only receive dispatches from the recent past, edited heavily for coherence.

Memory extends the same principle across years instead of nanoseconds. Every recollection is a reconstruction, not a replay—your brain rebuilds the scene each time, borrowing details, smoothing edges, sometimes inventing entirely. This sounds like a flaw, but it's closer to a mercy: we keep only what we can carry.

Maybe that's why people love photographs. A photograph is a promise against forgetting, a fixed point in all that drift. But the paradox is that staring at pictures of a moment often replaces the memory itself. The image survives; the living texture around it quietly evaporates.

So perhaps the quiet lesson of starlight is this: everything you have ever seen was already slipping away. Look anyway. Look closely, look kindly—the present is the only thing arriving.
